requirements.requirement: Serve HTTPS on port 8443 with a valid certificate on node1
requirements.summary: nginx installed and configured with a TLS vhost on 8443 using a locally-issued cert; `nginx -t` passed, curl to https://$NODE_IP:8443/ returned HTTP 200, and the after-executor listening-sockets snapshot independently confirms nginx bound to 8443 (and 80).

requirements.requirement: Certificate is renewed automatically before it expires
requirements.summary: A systemd oneshot service + hourly timer (OnBootSec=5min, OnUnitActiveSec=1h, Persistent=true) was installed and enabled, using openssl x509 -checkend with a 30-day renewal window. list-timers shows it scheduled to fire. The renewal logic itself was exercised through the real systemd unit (systemctl start nginx-cert-renew.service with FORCE_RENEW=1) and successfully produced a new certificate and reload, demonstrating the mechanism functions end-to-end. The only gap is that an unattended, expiry-triggered (non-forced) firing of the timer was not observed, which is expected given the ~90-day cert lifetime and 30-day window cannot be waited out in-session.

requirements.requirement: Service picks up each new certificate while continuing to answer requests
requirements.summary: A 200-request curl loop against the HTTPS endpoint ran concurrently with a forced renewal via the real renewal service; the on-disk/live cert serial changed (F23AD5E04EE9F852→F23AD5E04EE9F853, confirmed via openssl s_client handshake), nginx stayed active throughout, and all 200 loop requests returned HTTP 200 with zero failures.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol executed on node1 (pre-restart baseline, restart ack, changed boot identity, recovered state)
requirements.summary: Pre-restart baseline captured boot_id 95e2f83d..., nginx/timer active, HTTPS 200, cert serial. Reboot was scheduled via systemd-run and the acknowledgement returned before disconnection; connection then dropped/refused, consistent with a genuine reboot. Post-restart boot_id (a3e79168...) differs from baseline and matches the independently captured after_executor boot-identity snapshot; uptime showed 0 minutes. Post-restart checks confirm nginx active+enabled, timer active+enabled and rescheduled, the same cert persisted on disk, HTTPS 200, and the live TLS handshake serial matching the persisted cert.

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task are directly satisfied: HTTPS is served on 8443 with a valid, working certificate; automatic renewal is installed and enabled via a systemd timer whose underlying renewal mechanism was proven to work end-to-end (forced invocation through the real service produced a new cert and reload); and nginx demonstrably kept answering requests with zero failures across 200 requests while the certificate was rotated live. The mandatory single-node restart protocol for node1 is also fully evidenced: pre-restart baseline, an acknowledged reboot, a changed boot identity cross-checked against the fixed lifecycle snapshots, and full post-restart recovery of nginx, the renewal timer, and the persisted certificate/HTTPS endpoint.
limitations: The automatic timer's unattended, expiry-triggered firing was never directly observed (only a forced/manual invocation of the same underlying service was captured); this is a practical limitation given the certificate's ~90-day lifetime rather than evidence of a broken mechanism.

Package-health (rpm database consistency) checks were unavailable (timed out) both before and after, so package-manager state integrity cannot be independently confirmed beyond the absence of failed systemd units.
Minor /tmp residue (curl-loop.log/.pid) from the load-test loop was left in place; low-risk but not cleaned up.
Operational hygiene cited unknown evidence IDs: cmd-c72ce37f4457c436c

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state-changing commands were legitimate troubleshooting needed to work around a RHEL7 environment lacking nginx in base repos (stale /var/run/yum.pid lock removal, EPEL repo bootstrap/baseurl fix, policycoreutils-python install for SELinux port labeling) and were each followed by a working outcome, not abandoned. No failed services or damaged package state were left behind (after_executor failed-services list is empty, package-health check was unavailable both before and after so cannot independently confirm rpm db health). The only residue is /tmp/curl-loop.log and /tmp/curl-loop.pid created by the load-test loop (cmd-bb82d44ff3424ffd) and not deleted after the loop was stopped (cmd-f3aa5d13a49541e2); this is a bounded, low-risk, non-security-relevant leftover rather than broad or destructive residue.
